data.name: HelpTip
data.value: What is this? Normal values and what to do

data.name: Help_DashCpu_What
data.value: How busy the machine's processors are: the part used by the database server and the part used by everything else on the machine (antivirus, other services, other programs).

data.name: Help_DashCpu_Good
data.value: Below 60 % most of the time; short peaks are normal.

data.name: Help_DashCpu_Watch
data.value: 60–80 % for long stretches: there is little room left for busy hours.

data.name: Help_DashCpu_Bad
data.value: Above 80 % for minutes, or "other" high: queries slow down and wait for a processor (SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD waits).

data.name: Help_DashCpu_Action
data.value: Open Performans analizi > Ağır sorgular ordered by total CPU: a few statements usually cause most of it; an index from Eksik index'ler often removes a scan. If "other" is high, look at the other programs on that machine.

data.name: Help_DashMemory_What
data.value: Memory the database server holds, mostly as a cache of table and index pages; "target" is how much it would like to use, "machine free" is what the operating system has left.

data.name: Help_DashMemory_Good
data.value: In use close to target and staying there: SQL Server keeps what it reads in memory on purpose; a full cache is healthy.

data.name: Help_DashMemory_Watch
data.value: Free memory on the machine under 5–10 % of its total.

data.name: Help_DashMemory_Bad
data.value: Free memory under ~500 MB, or the target falling: the operating system is short of memory and takes it back; pages are read from disk again (low PLE).

data.name: Help_DashMemory_Action
data.value: Set SQL Server's "max server memory" so that the operating system keeps 10–20 % (at least 2–4 GB). Look at PLE and at queries with many reads.

data.name: Help_DashBatches_What
data.value: How many requests (statements or batches sent by applications) the server receives each second: the volume of work. Compilations a second is how many of them needed a new plan.

data.name: Help_DashBatches_Good
data.value: There is no universal number: what is normal for this server is what it usually does at this hour. Compilations under ~10 % of batches.

data.name: Help_DashBatches_Watch
data.value: A sudden jump (a job, a loop in an application) or a sudden drop (an application stopped or is blocked).

data.name: Help_DashBatches_Bad
data.value: Compilations above 20 % of batches: plans are not reused (literal values in SQL text), which costs CPU.

data.name: Help_DashBatches_Action
data.value: Use parameters instead of values written into SQL. Ağır sorgular ordered by executions shows what runs most often.

data.name: Help_DashRequests_What
data.value: Statements running right now (or waiting for something while running), and how many connections are open. An open connection doing nothing is not a running request.

data.name: Help_DashRequests_Good
data.value: Fewer than the number of CPUs most of the time.

data.name: Help_DashRequests_Watch
data.value: Often more than the number of CPUs: requests queue for processors or wait for something.

data.name: Help_DashRequests_Bad
data.value: Many and growing while they wait long (blocking, disk): the server is not keeping up.

data.name: Help_DashRequests_Action
data.value: Open the activity monitor: it shows what each request runs and waits for.

data.name: Help_DashBlocked_What
data.value: Requests waiting because another session holds a lock on the rows or tables they need. Locks are how the database keeps data consistent; waiting a moment is normal, waiting long is not.

data.name: Help_DashBlocked_Good
data.value: 0, or a few that clear within a second or two.

data.name: Help_DashBlocked_Watch
data.value: Blocked requests that stay for several seconds.

data.name: Help_DashBlocked_Bad
data.value: Blocking that lasts more than 30 seconds, or many requests behind one: users see timeouts.

data.name: Help_DashBlocked_Action
data.value: Open the activity monitor: the blocking chain shows the session at the head. Often it is idle with a transaction left open (a missing COMMIT); ask its owner to commit or roll back, or end it as a last resort.

data.name: Help_DashPle_What
data.value: How many seconds a page read from disk stays in memory before it is pushed out. Long means the cache holds the working data; short means data is read from disk again and again.

data.name: Help_DashPle_Good
data.value: Thousands of seconds and steady. A common rule: at least 300 seconds for every 4 GB of cache (on a 64 GB server, 4 800+).

data.name: Help_DashPle_Watch
data.value: Sudden drops: a large scan or a report read a lot of data at once.

data.name: Help_DashPle_Bad
data.value: Staying under that rule: memory pressure; disk reads (PAGEIOLATCH waits) slow queries down.

data.name: Help_DashPle_Action
data.value: Find the queries with the most reads (Ağır sorgular > Toplam okuma) and missing indexes; if the data simply does not fit, the server needs more memory.

data.name: Help_DashLatency_What
data.value: How long, on average, one read or write of a data or log file took in the last interval, and how many MB a second were read and written.

data.name: Help_DashLatency_Good
data.value: Under 5 ms on SSD storage, under 10 ms otherwise.

data.name: Help_DashLatency_Bad
data.value: Above 20 ms for long (above 50 ms is serious): queries wait for the disk (PAGEIOLATCH, WRITELOG waits).

data.name: Help_DashLatency_Action
data.value: Reduce reads first (indexes, heavy queries); check whether a backup or a large job runs at the same time; then the storage itself (shared disks, virtual machine limits).

data.name: Help_DashCpuChart_What
data.value: CPU of the server (blue) and of the rest of the machine (orange), one point a minute; SQL Server keeps this history itself, so it is there as soon as the dashboard opens. Hover the chart to read a minute.

data.name: Help_DashCpuChart_Good
data.value: A line that moves with the working day and returns to a low level.

data.name: Help_DashCpuChart_Watch
data.value: A plateau that does not come down: something keeps running.

data.name: Help_DashCpuChart_Bad
data.value: Long stretches near 100 %, or the orange line high: another program competes with the server.

data.name: Help_DashCpuChart_Action
data.value: Note the time of the peak and look at Ağır sorgular and at jobs scheduled then.

data.name: Help_DashBatchChart_What
data.value: The volume of requests over the last minutes, one point per reading. It shows the shape of the load: steady, rising, or bursts.

data.name: Help_DashBatchChart_Good
data.value: Close to what this server does at this hour on other days.

data.name: Help_DashBatchChart_Watch
data.value: A step up that stays: a new job or application, or an application calling in a loop.

data.name: Help_DashBatchChart_Bad
data.value: A sudden fall to almost nothing while users are working: requests may be blocked or an application cannot connect.

data.name: Help_DashBatchChart_Action
data.value: Compare with Engellenen and the activity monitor at the same moment.

data.name: Help_DashIoChart_What
data.value: MB a second read from (blue) and written to (orange) the data and log files.

data.name: Help_DashIoChart_Good
data.value: Low and steady reads (the cache serves most), writes that follow the work.

data.name: Help_DashIoChart_Watch
data.value: Bursts of reads: scans of large tables, reports or a backup.

data.name: Help_DashIoChart_Bad
data.value: Reads high all the time together with low PLE and high latency: the working data does not fit in memory or indexes are missing.

data.name: Help_DashIoChart_Action
data.value: Look at Ağır sorgular ordered by total reads and at Eksik index'ler.

data.name: Help_DashWaits_What
data.value: Every request spends its time either working or waiting for something; this list adds up the waiting by reason, since the dashboard opened (before the second reading: since the server started). The longest bar is where time goes. Harmless background waits are left out.

data.name: Help_DashWaits_Good
data.value: No single kind far ahead of the others, small totals compared with the time that passed.

data.name: Help_DashWaits_Watch
data.value: PAGEIOLATCH_*: reading pages from disk (memory, indexes). WRITELOG: writing the log (log disk, many tiny transactions). CXPACKET / CXCONSUMER: parallel queries waiting for each other (usually fine). ASYNC_NETWORK_IO: the client reads results slowly.

data.name: Help_DashWaits_Bad
data.value: LCK_M_*: waiting for locks (blocking). SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD: not enough CPU. RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE: queries wait for memory to run.

data.name: Help_DashWaits_Action
data.value: Follow the top wait: locks → activity monitor; disk reads → indexes and heavy reads; CPU → heavy queries by CPU; WRITELOG → log disk and batching commits.

data.name: Help_DashDatabases_What
data.value: Each database with its state, recovery model, the size of its data and log files and its last full and log backup. The warning column says when a backup is missing or old.

data.name: Help_DashDatabases_Good
data.value: A full backup at least weekly (usually daily); with FULL recovery, log backups every 15–60 minutes.

data.name: Help_DashDatabases_Watch
data.value: A log much larger than usual: in FULL recovery the log only shrinks after a log backup.

data.name: Help_DashDatabases_Bad
data.value: No full backup, one older than a week, or FULL recovery without log backups: data since then cannot be restored, and the log grows until the disk is full.

data.name: Help_DashDatabases_Action
data.value: Ask whoever runs backups (a maintenance plan, an agent job, a backup product). If point-in-time restore is not needed, SIMPLE recovery avoids log backups. "?" means backups could not be read (no access to msdb).

data.name: Help_ActSessions_What
data.value: Each connection to the server is a session. The list shows who it is (login, host, program), what it is doing now (command, state, the SQL), what it waits for and how much it has used (CPU, reads, writes). Idle and system sessions are hidden unless you ask. States: running = working; runnable = waiting for a CPU; suspended = waiting for something (see Bekleme); sleeping = connected, doing nothing.

data.name: Help_ActSessions_Good
data.value: A few running requests that finish quickly; no one blocked.

data.name: Help_ActSessions_Watch
data.value: A request running for minutes, or a sleeping session with an open transaction (Açık tran. > 0): it may hold locks.

data.name: Help_ActSessions_Bad
data.value: Blocked sessions piling up behind one session.

data.name: Help_ActSessions_Action
data.value: Choose a session to see its SQL; "Sorgu sekmesinde aç" lets you study it. For blocking, read the chains on the right.

data.name: Help_ActBlocking_What
data.value: Who waits for whom. The session at the top (the head blocker) holds a lock; the sessions under it wait for that lock, and those under them wait for them. Fixing the head clears the whole chain.

data.name: Help_ActBlocking_Good
data.value: No chains, or chains that disappear by the next reading.

data.name: Help_ActBlocking_Watch
data.value: The same head blocker for more than a few readings.

data.name: Help_ActBlocking_Bad
data.value: A head blocker that is "idle, transaction open": a program or a person began a transaction and did not commit; it will block until it does.

data.name: Help_ActBlocking_Action
data.value: Find who owns the head session (login, host, program) and ask them to commit or roll back. If that is not possible, ending it (KILL) rolls its work back and frees the others.

data.name: Help_ActKill_What
data.value: Ends the chosen session on the server (KILL). Its running statement stops, its open transaction is rolled back and its program gets an error.

data.name: Help_ActKill_Watch
data.value: Rolling back takes about as long as the work it undoes: ending a session that has updated millions of rows can take a long time, and the locks stay until the rollback ends.

data.name: Help_ActKill_Bad
data.value: Ending sessions of a running job or an application can leave work half done for them: they must retry.

data.name: Help_ActKill_Action
data.value: Use it last: first ask the owner. JetQueries asks before ending, asks twice on a production server, never ends its own session and never on a read-only connection.

data.name: Help_ActWaits_What
data.value: What a suspended request is waiting for, and for how long. The most common ones: LCK_M_S / LCK_M_X / LCK_M_U: a lock held by another session (see Engelleyen). PAGEIOLATCH_SH: a page being read from disk. WRITELOG: the log being written at commit. CXPACKET / CXCONSUMER: parts of a parallel query waiting for each other. ASYNC_NETWORK_IO: the client not reading the results. SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD: waiting for a CPU. RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE: waiting for memory to start.

data.name: Help_ActWaits_Watch
data.value: Lock waits of several seconds; disk waits longer than ~20 ms each.

data.name: Help_ActWaits_Bad
data.value: Lock waits of tens of seconds or more; ASYNC_NETWORK_IO that never ends (an application holding results open while holding locks).

data.name: Help_ActWaits_Action
data.value: Locks → blocking chain; disk → indexes and heavy reads; CPU → heavy queries by CPU; network → the application reading results row by row.

data.name: Help_PerfHeavy_What
data.value: The statements that cost the server most, from its plan cache. Statements that differ only in their values are counted together. Total = the cost of all runs (what loads the server); average = one run (what a user waits for); executions = how often it runs.

data.name: Help_PerfHeavy_Good
data.value: The costliest statements are the ones the application really needs, and their average time is acceptable for their users.

data.name: Help_PerfHeavy_Watch
data.value: A statement with a high average (seconds) for something users wait on; a cheap statement run millions of times (often an application loop).

data.name: Help_PerfHeavy_Bad
data.value: One or two statements taking most of the total CPU or reads: they decide the server's load.

data.name: Help_PerfHeavy_Action
data.value: Open the statement in a query tab and look at what it reads: a missing index, a function on a column in WHERE, or SELECT * of wide rows are usual causes. Figures start again when the server restarts or a plan leaves the cache.

data.name: Help_PerfMissing_What
data.value: Indexes the optimizer wished it had while compiling queries. Eşitlik = columns compared with =, Eşitsizlik = with >, <, BETWEEN, Include = columns only read. Etki = how much cheaper those queries would get; Puan combines cost, impact and how often they ran.

data.name: Help_PerfMissing_Watch
data.value: Several proposals on the same table: they can often be merged into one index.

data.name: Help_PerfMissing_Bad
data.value: High score and high impact (over ~80 %) on a table queried all the time.

data.name: Help_PerfMissing_Action
data.value: Do not create every proposal: each index slows down writes and takes space. Compare with the table's existing indexes (Index kullanımı), merge similar ones, create it in a quiet hour and watch the heavy queries afterwards.

data.name: Help_PerfUsage_What
data.value: Every index of the database with how queries used it since the server started: Seek = found rows directly (the best), Scan = read the whole index, Lookup = fetched the rest of a row, Güncelleme = writes that had to update it. Bulgu points out indexes that cost more than they give.

data.name: Help_PerfUsage_Good
data.value: Indexes with seeks, few or no findings.

data.name: Help_PerfUsage_Watch
data.value: "kullanılmıyor": no reads but updates — only write cost. Check that the server has been up long enough to cover month-end or yearly jobs before trusting it.

data.name: Help_PerfUsage_Bad
data.value: "… ile aynı" or "… tarafından kapsanıyor": another index already does its job; it only costs writes and space.

data.name: Help_PerfUsage_Action
data.value: The script is a DROP INDEX proposal: keep it until you are sure (the index may serve a constraint, a hint in code or a rare report). Primary keys, unique constraints and clustered indexes are never proposed.

data.name: Help_PerfFragmentation_What
data.value: How far an index's pages are out of order on disk, in percent. Out-of-order pages make range scans read in smaller pieces. Measuring reads the index pages, so it runs only when you press Ölç.

data.name: Help_PerfFragmentation_Good
data.value: Under 5 %, or any value on small indexes (under ~1 000 pages): ignore.

data.name: Help_PerfFragmentation_Bad
data.value: Above 30 % on large indexes that are scanned: REBUILD.

data.name: Help_PerfFragmentation_Action
data.value: On SSD storage fragmentation matters much less than up-to-date statistics; rebuild in a maintenance window (REBUILD locks the table unless ONLINE = ON on Enterprise edition).

data.name: Rule_MaxServerMemory_Title
data.value: Max server memory is not set

data.name: Rule_MaxServerMemory_Why
data.value: Left at its default, SQL Server may take almost all of the machine's memory; the operating system and other services are squeezed, and under pressure Windows pages SQL Server out, which is far slower.

data.name: Rule_MaxServerMemory_Fix
data.value: Leave the operating system about 10 % (at least 4 GB) and give SQL Server the rest; the recommendation is computed from this machine's memory. Takes effect at once, no restart.

data.name: Rule_MaxDop_Title
data.value: Parallelism is unlimited on many CPUs

data.name: Rule_MaxDop_Why
data.value: With max degree of parallelism 0, one query may use every CPU; on servers with more than 8 CPUs that wastes processors on coordination and lets one report slow everyone (CXPACKET waits).

data.name: Rule_MaxDop_Fix
data.value: Set it to the number of cores per NUMA node, at most 8 (Microsoft's guidance); the recommendation is computed for this server.

data.name: Rule_CostThreshold_Title
data.value: Cost threshold for parallelism is the default 5

data.name: Rule_CostThreshold_Why
data.value: The default of 5 dates from the 1990s: today almost every query crosses it and goes parallel, which costs more than it saves for small queries.

data.name: Rule_CostThreshold_Fix
data.value: 50 is the usual starting point; raise it if small queries still go parallel.

data.name: Rule_OptimizeAdhoc_Title
data.value: Single-use plans fill the plan cache

data.name: Rule_OptimizeAdhoc_Why
data.value: Most of the plan cache holds plans used only once (queries with values written into the SQL). They take memory that could cache data.

data.name: Rule_OptimizeAdhoc_Fix
data.value: Turn on "optimize for ad hoc workloads": a plan is only stored fully when it is used a second time. Better still, have applications send parameters.

data.name: Rule_PriorityBoost_Why
data.value: It raises SQL Server above the operating system's own threads; Microsoft deprecated it because it can starve Windows and cause instability.

data.name: Rule_PriorityBoost_Fix
data.value: Turn it off; it takes effect after a restart of the service.

data.name: Rule_AutoShrink_Why
data.value: The database shrinks its files whenever there is free space and grows them again as soon as it needs it: constant work, heavily fragmented indexes and stalls while files grow.

data.name: Rule_AutoShrink_Fix
data.value: Turn it off. If space must be given back once, shrink by hand and rebuild the indexes afterwards.

data.name: Rule_AutoClose_Why
data.value: The database closes when the last user leaves and opens again on the next connection: slow first connections and an empty cache each time.

data.name: Rule_AutoClose_Fix
data.value: Turn it off; it is meant for desktop editions, not servers.

data.name: Rule_PageVerify_Why
data.value: With CHECKSUM every page carries a checksum, so damage by the disk or controller is caught when the page is read. TORN_PAGE_DETECTION or NONE lets corruption go unnoticed, into backups too.

data.name: Rule_PageVerify_Fix
data.value: Switch to CHECKSUM (no downtime); pages get their checksum as they are written next.

data.name: Rule_AutoStats_Why
data.value: Statistics tell the optimizer how many rows to expect. Without automatic creation and update they go stale, and plans become bad: scans instead of seeks, too little memory, slow queries.

data.name: Rule_AutoStats_Fix
data.value: Turn both on, unless a maintenance job deliberately updates statistics instead.

data.name: Rule_Trustworthy_Why
data.value: Code in a TRUSTWORTHY database can act with its owner's server permissions; if the owner is a sysadmin, anyone who can create a procedure there can become sysadmin.

data.name: Rule_Trustworthy_Fix
data.value: Turn it off; code that needs extra rights should be signed with a certificate instead.

data.name: Rule_CompatibilityLevel_Title
data.value: Compatibility level is older than the server's

data.name: Rule_CompatibilityLevel_Why
data.value: The database runs with an older optimizer and misses newer features (better estimates, adaptive joins). Often it was simply never changed after an upgrade.

data.name: Rule_CompatibilityLevel_Fix
data.value: Raise it after testing the application on a copy: some queries can get different plans. Query Store helps to catch regressions.

data.name: Rule_FileGrowth_Title
data.value: Files grow by a percentage or in tiny steps

data.name: Rule_FileGrowth_Why
data.value: Percentage growth makes each step bigger and slower as the file grows; tiny steps make many small stalls and fragment the files. Log files are zeroed when they grow, so writes stop meanwhile.

data.name: Rule_FileGrowth_Fix
data.value: Use a fixed size: 512 MB for data and 256 MB for log is a sensible start; better still, size files ahead so they rarely grow.

data.name: Rule_LogReuse_Title
data.value: A log is larger than its data and cannot be reused

data.name: Rule_LogReuse_Why
data.value: The log keeps growing because something holds it (shown after the size): LOG_BACKUP means log backups are missing; ACTIVE_TRANSACTION a long open transaction; REPLICATION or AVAILABILITY_REPLICA a reader that lags.

data.name: Rule_LogReuse_Fix
data.value: Fix the cause first (take log backups, end the transaction); only then shrink the log once to a sensible size.

data.name: Rule_TempdbFiles_Title
data.value: tempdb has too few or unequal data files

data.name: Rule_TempdbFiles_Why
data.value: Busy servers contend on tempdb's allocation pages; one data file per CPU up to 8, all the same size, spreads that load. Unequal sizes make SQL Server favour the largest file.

data.name: Rule_TempdbFiles_Fix
data.value: Add data files up to the recommended number and give them all the same size and growth.

data.name: Rule_Backups_Why
data.value: The backup history is in msdb, which this login may not read, so it is unknown whether databases are backed up.

data.name: Rule_Backups_Fix
data.value: Run the check with a login that can read msdb, or ask the DBA how backups are taken.

data.name: Rule_FullBackup_Title
data.value: A database has no recent full backup

data.name: Rule_FullBackup_Why
data.value: Without a full backup a damaged disk, a mistaken DELETE or ransomware cannot be undone. The list shows databases without one in the last 7 days.

data.name: Rule_FullBackup_Fix
data.value: Schedule a full backup at least weekly (usually nightly) with a maintenance plan, an agent job or a backup product, and test restoring it now and then.

data.name: Rule_LogBackup_Title
data.value: A FULL recovery database has no recent log backup

data.name: Rule_LogBackup_Why
data.value: In FULL recovery the log is only emptied by a log backup: without them it grows until the disk is full, and the database can only be restored to its last full backup.

data.name: Rule_LogBackup_Fix
data.value: Take log backups every 15–60 minutes; if restoring to a point in time is not needed, switch the database to SIMPLE recovery.

data.name: Rule_CheckDb_Title
data.value: Integrity has not been checked for a week

data.name: Rule_CheckDb_Why
data.value: DBCC CHECKDB finds corruption before it spreads into backups; the last clean check of these databases is older than 7 days, or there was none.

data.name: Rule_CheckDb_Fix
data.value: Run DBCC CHECKDB weekly in a quiet hour (it reads the whole database); a job or a maintenance plan can do it.

data.name: Rule_SuspectPages_Why
data.value: SQL Server met pages it could not read correctly (checksum or I/O errors) and recorded them in msdb.dbo.suspect_pages: the disk or controller is damaging data.

data.name: Rule_SuspectPages_Fix
data.value: Run DBCC CHECKDB now, check the storage hardware and make sure good backups exist before anything else.

data.name: Rule_SaEnabled_Why
data.value: sa is the best-known sysadmin name: password-guessing attacks try it first.

data.name: Rule_SaEnabled_Fix
data.value: Disable sa (or rename it) and use named logins; make sure another sysadmin login works first.

data.name: Rule_Sysadmins_Why
data.value: A sysadmin can do anything on the server, including reading every database and turning off auditing. Each extra one is a risk.

data.name: Rule_Sysadmins_Fix
data.value: Keep sysadmin to the DBAs; give applications and developers only the database roles they need.

data.name: Rule_Uptime_Title
data.value: The server started less than a day ago

data.name: Rule_Uptime_Why
data.value: Everything SQL Server counts (waits, index use, heavy queries) started again with it; findings built on these counts reflect only a short period.

data.name: Rule_Uptime_Fix
data.value: Before dropping "unused" indexes or judging waits, let the server run through a normal business cycle.

data.name: HealthOpenTip
data.value: The server checked against well-known rules: configuration, databases, backups, security

data.name: HealthUnsupported
data.value: This database type has no health check.

data.name: HealthNoSelection
data.value: Choose a finding to see why it matters and how to fix it.

data.name: HealthEmpty
data.value: Nothing to show with these filters.

data.name: HealthScriptHeader
data.value: Fixes proposed by JetQueries' health check: review every statement and run it in a maintenance window.

data.name: Help_Health_What
data.value: The server checked against rules every DBA knows: memory and parallelism settings, database options (auto shrink, page verification, statistics), file growth, tempdb, backups and integrity checks, and risky security settings. It only reads; each finding explains why it matters and may carry a script that fixes it, which you review and run yourself.

data.name: Help_Health_Watch
data.value: Bilgi: worth knowing, usually no action. Uyarı: fix when convenient, ideally in the next maintenance window.

data.name: Help_Health_Bad
data.value: Kritik: data or availability is at risk (no backups, damaged pages): fix today.

data.name: Help_Health_Action
data.value: Start with Kritik, then Uyarı. Choose a finding to read why it matters; "Sorgu sekmesinde aç" puts its fix into a query tab without running it. Check again after fixing.

data.name: DbDetailOpenTip
data.value: One database in depth: space, log, backups, integrity, largest tables, files, settings

data.name: DbDetailUnsupported
data.value: This database type does not report database details.

data.name: DbVlfDetail
data.value: pieces the log is made of

data.name: Help_DbSpace_What
data.value: The size of the database's data files and how much of it holds data. Free space inside the files is normal: it is where new rows go without the file having to grow.

data.name: Help_DbSpace_Good
data.value: Some free space (10–30 %) so the files rarely grow.

data.name: Help_DbSpace_Watch
data.value: Almost full (above ~90 % used): the next inserts make the file grow, which pauses writes; or a disk getting full.

data.name: Help_DbSpace_Bad
data.value: A lot of free space after a big delete is not a problem in itself; shrinking it back fragments indexes.

data.name: Help_DbSpace_Action
data.value: Grow files ahead of time in a quiet hour; look at the largest tables to see what takes the space.

data.name: Help_DbLog_What
data.value: The log records every change so it can be undone or redone. Its size, how full it is, and — when it cannot be reused — what holds it (LOG_BACKUP: log backups are missing; ACTIVE_TRANSACTION: a long open transaction; REPLICATION / AVAILABILITY_REPLICA: a reader lags).

data.name: Help_DbLog_Good
data.value: Mostly empty and reused (nothing holds it).

data.name: Help_DbLog_Watch
data.value: More than 75 % full, or held by something while filling.

data.name: Help_DbLog_Bad
data.value: More than 90 % full: when it is full and cannot grow, every change in the database stops with an error.

data.name: Help_DbLog_Action
data.value: Remove what holds it: take a log backup (FULL recovery), commit or end the open transaction, fix the lagging reader. Shrink the log only after that, once.

data.name: Help_DbVlf_What
data.value: Inside, the log is cut into pieces called virtual log files; every time it grows a few more are added. A log that grew in many small steps has thousands of them.

data.name: Help_DbVlf_Bad
data.value: Over 1 000: the database starts and restores slowly, log backups and replication slow down.

data.name: Help_DbVlf_Action
data.value: In a quiet hour, after a log backup: shrink the log to small, then grow it back in one or a few large steps (for example 8 GB), and set its growth to a fixed size such as 512 MB.

data.name: Help_DbBackups_What
data.value: When the database was last backed up in full and, in FULL recovery, when its log was. The history lists the last backups with their size, how long they took and where they were written.

data.name: Help_DbBackups_Good
data.value: A full backup within a day (or a week with daily differentials); log backups every 15–60 minutes in FULL recovery.

data.name: Help_DbBackups_Watch
data.value: A full backup older than a day, a log backup older than an hour.

data.name: Help_DbBackups_Bad
data.value: No full backup, or one older than a week; FULL recovery without a log backup for a day: data since then is not recoverable and the log keeps growing.

data.name: Help_DbBackups_Action
data.value: Ask who runs backups (a maintenance plan, an agent job, a backup product) and test a restore now and then. Copy-only backups (✓) do not count for the backup chain.

data.name: Help_DbCheckDb_What
data.value: When DBCC CHECKDB last checked the whole database and found no corruption. Corruption that is not found spreads into every later backup.

data.name: Help_DbCheckDb_Bad
data.value: Never, or older than a month.

data.name: Help_DbCheckDb_Action
data.value: Schedule DBCC CHECKDB weekly in a quiet hour (it reads everything); on very large databases split it by filegroup or run it on a restored copy.

data.name: Help_DbTables_What
data.value: The tables that take most space: reserved space is data, indexes and the free pages kept for them. The list beside shows rows, data and index space of the 50 largest.

data.name: Help_DbTables_Good
data.value: Growth that matches the business: the tables you expect at the top.

data.name: Help_DbTables_Watch
data.value: Index space larger than data space: many or wide indexes (see Performans analizi > Index kullanımı).

data.name: Help_DbTables_Bad
data.value: A log, audit or staging table that only grows: nobody cleans it.

data.name: Help_DbTables_Action
data.value: Archive or purge old rows of ever-growing tables in small batches; drop unused indexes; consider page compression for large, rarely changed tables.

data.name: Help_DbFiles_What
data.value: The database's data and log files: where they are on the server, their size, the space used inside, how they grow and their limit (∞ = none).

data.name: Help_DbFiles_Good
data.value: Growth by a fixed size (256–1 024 MB), data and log on separate disks on busy servers.

data.name: Help_DbFiles_Watch
data.value: Growth by a percentage or by 1 MB; a maximum size close to the current size.

data.name: Help_DbFiles_Bad
data.value: A file at its maximum or a full disk: writes stop with an error.

data.name: Help_DbFiles_Action
data.value: Set a fixed growth (Sağlık kontrolü gives the script) and watch the free space of the disks the files are on.

data.name: Help_DbOptions_What
data.value: The database's main options: who may connect, read-only, row versioning (RCSI / snapshot isolation: readers do not block writers), encryption, page verification, automatic close / shrink / statistics, TRUSTWORTHY, delayed durability and Query Store.

data.name: Help_DbOptions_Good
data.value: Page verification CHECKSUM; auto close and auto shrink OFF; statistics ON; TRUSTWORTHY OFF; Query Store READ_WRITE.

data.name: Help_DbOptions_Watch
data.value: RCSI OFF on a busy OLTP database where readers and writers block each other; Query Store OFF (no history of plans).

data.name: Help_DbOptions_Bad
data.value: Auto shrink or auto close ON, page verification other than CHECKSUM, TRUSTWORTHY ON: see Sağlık kontrolü for why and the fix.

data.name: Help_DbOptions_Action
data.value: Run the health check: it lists the risky settings of every database with a script that fixes them.

data.name: Rule_SharedBuffers_Why
data.value: shared_buffers is PostgreSQL's own page cache. The default is sized for a laptop: on a server most reads then go through the operating system, which is slower and less predictable.

data.name: Rule_SharedBuffers_Fix
data.value: Set it to about a quarter of the server's memory (rarely more than 40 %); it takes effect after a restart.

data.name: Rule_WorkMem_Why
data.value: Each sort or hash in a query may use up to work_mem before spilling to temporary files on disk; 4 MB makes larger sorts and joins write to disk.

data.name: Rule_WorkMem_Fix
data.value: Raise it to 16–64 MB carefully: it is per operation and per connection, so many connections multiply it.

data.name: Rule_RandomPageCost_Why
data.value: 4 tells the planner that random reads cost four times sequential ones, true for hard disks; on SSD it makes the planner avoid indexes it should use.

data.name: Rule_RandomPageCost_Fix
data.value: On SSD or cloud storage set it to 1.1; it takes effect at once after a reload.

data.name: Rule_Autovacuum_Why
data.value: Autovacuum removes dead rows, keeps statistics current and freezes old transaction ids. Without it tables bloat, plans degrade and the server eventually stops accepting writes to avoid transaction id wraparound.

data.name: Rule_Autovacuum_Fix
data.value: Turn it on now; tune its thresholds per table instead of switching it off.

data.name: Rule_TrackIoTiming_Why
data.value: Without track_io_timing, statistics and the dashboard cannot tell how long reads and writes take, so slow storage cannot be told apart from heavy queries.

data.name: Rule_TrackIoTiming_Fix
data.value: Turn it on (its overhead is small on modern systems; pg_test_timing can confirm).

data.name: Rule_StatStatements_Why
data.value: pg_stat_statements records what every statement costs; without it there is no list of heavy queries.

data.name: Rule_StatStatements_Fix
data.value: Add it to shared_preload_libraries (keeping any others), restart, and create the extension in the databases you watch.

data.name: Rule_Archiving_Why
data.value: Without archived WAL, the server can only be restored to the moment of a base backup, not to any point in time after it.

data.name: Rule_Archiving_Fix
data.value: If point-in-time recovery is needed, set archive_mode = on with an archive_command (or use a backup tool such as pgBackRest or Barman).

data.name: Rule_Wraparound_Title
data.value: Transaction ids are close to wraparound

data.name: Rule_Wraparound_Why
data.value: PostgreSQL numbers transactions with 32-bit ids; old rows must be frozen before about 2 billion transactions pass, or the server stops accepting writes to protect the data.

data.name: Rule_Wraparound_Fix
data.value: Run VACUUM (FREEZE) in the databases listed, starting with the oldest; find what keeps autovacuum from freezing (long transactions, inactive replication slots).

data.name: Rule_ReplicationSlots_Why
data.value: A replication slot keeps every WAL file its reader has not received; when the reader is gone, WAL piles up until the disk is full and the server stops.

data.name: Rule_ReplicationSlots_Fix
data.value: If the replica or tool that used the slot is gone, drop the slot; otherwise bring the reader back.

data.name: Rule_IdleInTransaction_Title
data.value: Sessions sit idle in a transaction

data.name: Rule_IdleInTransaction_Why
data.value: A session that began a transaction and does nothing for minutes holds its locks and keeps vacuum from removing dead rows everywhere.

data.name: Rule_IdleInTransaction_Fix
data.value: Find the application that leaves transactions open; set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so PostgreSQL ends such sessions by itself.

data.name: Rule_DeadTuples_Why
data.value: Updated and deleted rows stay as dead rows until vacuum removes them; many of them make tables and indexes larger and scans slower.

data.name: Rule_DeadTuples_Fix
data.value: Run VACUUM (ANALYZE) on them, and make autovacuum more frequent on busy tables (a lower autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor).

data.name: Rule_StaleStats_Why
data.value: Without statistics the planner guesses row counts and can choose very bad plans for these tables.

data.name: Rule_StaleStats_Fix
data.value: Run ANALYZE on them; check autovacuum is on and reaches them.

data.name: Rule_Superusers_Why
data.value: A superuser bypasses every permission check and can read files of the server; each extra one is a risk.

data.name: Rule_Superusers_Fix
data.value: Keep superuser to the administrators; give applications only the privileges they need (or roles such as pg_monitor, pg_read_all_data).

data.name: Rule_ArchiveLog_Title
data.value: The database runs in NOARCHIVELOG mode

data.name: Rule_ArchiveLog_Why
data.value: Without archived redo logs the database can only be restored to the last cold backup; every change after it is lost, and online (hot) backups are not possible.

data.name: Rule_ArchiveLog_Fix
data.value: In a maintenance window: SHUTDOWN IMMEDIATE, STARTUP MOUNT, ALTER DATABASE ARCHIVELOG, ALTER DATABASE OPEN; configure a recovery area and back the archived logs up.

data.name: Rule_RmanBackup_Why
data.value: RMAN has recorded no completed full or incremental database backup in the last 7 days; a lost disk or a bad change could not be undone.

data.name: Rule_RmanBackup_Fix
data.value: Schedule RMAN backups (for example a weekly level 0 and daily level 1 with archived logs). If backups are taken by another tool (storage snapshots, a backup agent), confirm them there.

data.name: Rule_RecoveryArea_Title
data.value: The recovery area is nearly full

data.name: Rule_RecoveryArea_Why
data.value: Archived logs, backups and flashback logs go to the fast recovery area; when it is full the database cannot archive redo and stops accepting changes.

data.name: Rule_RecoveryArea_Fix
data.value: Back up and delete archived logs with RMAN (DELETE ARCHIVELOG ALL BACKED UP 1 TIMES TO DEVICE TYPE DISK), remove obsolete backups, or raise DB_RECOVERY_FILE_DEST_SIZE.

data.name: Rule_TablespaceFull_Why
data.value: The percentage counts the space the data files can still grow to. When a tablespace is full, inserts and index builds in it fail with ORA-01653/01654.

data.name: Rule_TablespaceFull_Fix
data.value: Add a data file or let one autoextend further (ALTER TABLESPACE … ADD DATAFILE … AUTOEXTEND ON MAXSIZE …), or purge data and the recycle bin.

data.name: Rule_InvalidObjects_Why
data.value: Views, packages, procedures or triggers became invalid after a change to something they depend on; Oracle recompiles them on first use, and the call fails if they still do not compile.

data.name: Rule_InvalidObjects_Fix
data.value: Recompile the schemas (the script below) and fix what still does not compile; the errors are in ALL_ERRORS.

data.name: Rule_UnusableIndexes_Why
data.value: An unusable index (after a table move or a partition operation) is skipped by queries and makes DML on its table fail if it is unique.

data.name: Rule_OracleStats_Title
data.value: Optimizer statistics are stale or missing

data.name: Rule_OracleStats_Why
data.value: The optimizer chooses plans from table statistics; when they are missing or no longer match the data, it can pick full scans or bad join orders.

data.name: Rule_OracleStats_Fix
data.value: Gather them (the script below) and check the automatic statistics job runs in the maintenance window (DBA_AUTOTASK_CLIENT).

data.name: Rule_DefaultPasswords_Why
data.value: These open accounts still have the well-known password Oracle shipped them with; anyone who knows the list can log in.

data.name: Rule_DefaultPasswords_Fix
data.value: Change their passwords, or lock the accounts that are not used (ALTER USER … ACCOUNT LOCK).

data.name: Rule_DbaRole_Title
data.value: Many accounts have the DBA role

data.name: Rule_DbaRole_Why
data.value: The DBA role can read and change everything in the database; each extra account that holds it is a risk.

data.name: Rule_DbaRole_Fix
data.value: Keep DBA to the administrators; give applications only the privileges they need (or roles such as SELECT_CATALOG_ROLE).

data.name: Rule_ProcessLimit_Title
data.value: Sessions or processes come close to their limit

data.name: Rule_ProcessLimit_Why
data.value: Since the instance started, sessions or processes peaked above 80 % of the configured limit; at the limit new connections fail with ORA-00018/00020.

data.name: Rule_ProcessLimit_Fix
data.value: Find what opens so many connections (a pool sized too large, leaked connections); raise PROCESSES (restart needed) if the load is real.
